fields.expected: The work of mine that connects most directly to identity and fraud is a Playwright-based job-application agent I built in TypeScript and Node. The interesting part was not making the browser do things, it was deciding where automation should stop. A wrong action there can submit a real application, fabricate an answer, or wrongly fill a legal or demographic field, so I put every mutating capability behind fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED and FORM_FILL_ENABLED, used SQLite as the single source of truth because state divergence across processes is where browser automation gets dangerous, and made free-text and demographic fields architecturally impossible to autofill. I also built a validation ladder from unit-confirmed to live-mutation-confirmed, because passing against a local fixture does not mean a capability works against reality. Workday and iCIMS are detected and skipped rather than handled unreliably. I think about adversarial automation from the other side of Persona's problem, which is part of why the work interests me. Separately, at Intelehealth I built an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard, which is where I started treating whether an output should be trusted as the harder technical problem than generating it.
